clue.text: New tutor gets one wrong? It's hard to say

definitions.text: New tutor gets one wrong? It's hard to say

parts.words: New tutor gets one wrong? It's hard to say
parts.note: try saying 'new tutor' fast and often and you trip over it: the clue describes a phrase built to make the speaker stumble

explanation.surface: A newly hired teacher marks one answer wrong, and the pupil protests that the question was hard to put into words.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's hard to say' reads as 'it's hard to tell', but it is literal: the thing is difficult to pronounce, and 'new tutor' itself is a small example.
explanation.definitionFit: A phrase deliberately difficult to articulate quickly, like 'new tutor', is exactly this kind of verbal trap.

clue.text: A certain sort of sail, in the trend of Tusitala's tale

indicators.note: in puts the first pieces inside the following word

parts.note: taken as written
certain means sure

indicators.note: sort of says the following word is a version of itself, its letters jumbled

explanation.surface: A kind of sail fashionable in Stevenson's story.
explanation.walkthrough: Tusitala ('teller of tales') was the Samoans' name for Robert Louis Stevenson; the comma hides that 'sort of' only jumbles the one word beside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Stevenson's pirate adventure with Long John Silver is his best-known story.

clue.text: Point to area of oyster-production

parts.note: N for north is a point of the compass
an acre is a unit of area

explanation.surface: Indicating a region where oysters are farmed.
explanation.definitionFit: Mother-of-pearl, the lustrous lining layer an oyster secretes, is its product.

clue.text: Fun can be so noisy-when Leo's rising?

definitions.text: Fun can be so noisy-when Leo's rising?

parts.words: Fun can be so noisy-when Leo's rising?
parts.note: fun can be very loud and boisterous; Leo is the lion, and when he gets up his roar goes up too

explanation.surface: Merriment gets very loud, perhaps under the star sign Leo.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half splits the answer: rising gives UP and Leo the lion gives ROAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Boisterous laughter and very loud merriment are described by this adjective.

clue.text: To whom his love, princess that is, sold her heart

definitions.text: To whom his love, princess that is, sold her heart

parts.words: To whom his love, princess that is, sold her heart
parts.note: his love is the Irish princess of the legend, and her name is 'that is' (IE) with SOLD as its heart

explanation.surface: A princess sold her heart to the man she loved.
explanation.walkthrough: The princess is Isolde: I(SOLD)E, 'that is' around 'sold'. She is the beloved of the Cornish knight in the Arthurian romance.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cornish knight of Arthurian legend whose tragic beloved was the Irish princess Isolde.

clue.text: Heeded not what might be doing round about

indicators.note: round says the reworked word encloses the next piece
what might be suggests the word could become something else, its letters reworked

parts.note: RE is Latin for about, concerning

explanation.surface: Someone paid no attention to what might be going on around them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'doing round about' reads as idle loafing, but 'round' is a container signal: the jumbled IGNOD wraps the Latin 'about'.
explanation.definitionFit: To pay no attention to something is to disregard it, the opposite of heeding.

clue.text: It takes a shopkeeper's money to work the land

definitions.meaning: the cash drawer in a shop

explanation.definitionFit: A shop's cash register holds the takings, and the same word means to cultivate farmland.

clue.text: Sapper's account of the return

parts.note: sappers are the Royal Engineers, RE
a version is one account of events

explanation.surface: A military engineer gives his story of coming home.
explanation.walkthrough: A sapper is a soldier of the Royal Engineers, abbreviated RE.
explanation.definitionFit: A going back to an earlier state, or property passing back to its owner, is a return.

clue.text: The pound in your wallet is the Bank of England's

definitions.text: The pound in your wallet is the Bank of England's

parts.words: The pound in your wallet is the Bank of England's
parts.note: a banknote carries the Bank's written pledge 'I promise to pay the bearer on demand', so the paper is the Bank's IOU

explanation.surface: The money you carry really belongs to the Bank of England.
explanation.walkthrough: English banknotes are printed 'I promise to pay the bearer on demand the sum of one pound', so a pound note is the Bank's written pledge.
explanation.definitionFit: A written pledge to pay a sum on demand is exactly what a banknote is.

clue.text: Sally by Wordsworth

definitions.meaning: a sally is a short trip or outing
Wordsworth wrote a long poem titled The ... (1814)

explanation.definitionFit: A sally is a brief outing or trip, and the same word is the title of a long Wordsworth poem.

clue.text: The going's proverbially rough for him, true

definitions.text: The going's proverbially rough for him, true

parts.words: The going's proverbially rough for him, true
parts.note: the proverb is 'the course of true love never did run smooth', so the person whose going is rough is the one in love

explanation.surface: Someone is having a hard time of it, and the speaker agrees that this is proverbial.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue rests on Shakespeare's line 'The course of true love never did run smooth'; 'going' stands for course and 'true' points to true love.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb says true love's course is never smooth, so its hard going belongs to the person in love, a sweetheart.

clue.text: Scottish one is back in Italy

definitions.note: the definition describes a place, a city located in Italy

indicators.note: back tells us the two pieces are read from right to left

parts.note: ane is the Scots word for one

explanation.surface: A Scot who has been away has returned to Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns ANE and IS together, giving SI then ENA.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tuscan city famous for its Palio horse race is located in Italy.

clue.text: Revolution — what a performance!

definitions.meaning: a revolution is one full rotation
a music-hall act or routine is a performance

explanation.definitionFit: One complete rotation is a revolution, and a variety artiste's act on stage is also called this.

clue.text: Stuff with head of cauliflower and butter

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, here taken from the vegetable

parts.note: a ram butts with its head, so it is a butter

explanation.surface: A recipe: fill something with cauliflower florets and butter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'butter' is not the dairy spread but one who butts, a ram.
explanation.definitionFit: To stuff something is to pack it full, the same as forcing it full of contents.

clue.text: I get dinner cooked. It goes in the pot

indicators.note: cooked suggests the words are prepared and transformed, rearranged here

explanation.surface: Someone making the evening meal adds something to the saucepan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cooked' reorders the letters of I GET DINNER.
explanation.definitionFit: Anything that goes into the pot is a component of the dish, such as onion or salt.

clue.text: Red rather than green, this salad ?

definitions.text: Red rather than green, this salad ?

parts.words: Red rather than green, this salad ?
parts.note: a salad named after a nationality whose people were politically Red, in place of the green leaves usual in a salad

explanation.surface: A salad that is red instead of the expected green.
explanation.walkthrough: Red is the old shorthand for Communist, so the salad is named for the Soviet country rather than for its colour.
explanation.definitionFit: A diced vegetable salad in mayonnaise bears the name of the country long associated with the Communist Reds.

clue.text: Backed up and played around

indicators.note: around says the synonym for played encloses the other word

parts.note: to sport is to play
taken as written

explanation.surface: Something was reversed and fooled around with.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backed up' seems to be one phrase, but 'up' is the piece that goes inside SPORTED.
explanation.definitionFit: To back someone is to bear them up, endorse or hold them up.

clue.text: Smart fellows bring false report from lions' den

parts.note: the Biblical Daniel was thrown into the lions' den; Dan is his short name
the false report from the den would be that he dies, as Daniel in fact survived

explanation.surface: Fashionable men spreading a lie about what happened among the lions.
explanation.walkthrough: The false report is the sentence 'Dan dies': in the Book of Daniel he came out of the lions' den unharmed.
explanation.definitionFit: Men excessively concerned with elegant dress are fops, the smartly turned-out fellows of the clue.

clue.text: When Ezra introduces himself, shut up!

parts.note: someone introducing himself says 'I'm', followed by his name
Ezra Pound was the American poet

explanation.surface: Someone tells the poet Ezra to be quiet just as he starts introducing himself.
explanation.walkthrough: Ezra Pound introducing himself would say 'I'm Pound'. 'shut up' is not a rude command but means confine.
explanation.definitionFit: To shut up something, such as stray cattle or seized goods, is to confine it in an enclosure or official custody.

clue.text: Times are rotten? One of them would sound so.

definitions.text: Times are rotten? One of them would sound so.

parts.words: Times are rotten? One of them would sound so.
parts.note: the periods of time are ten-year spans, and one of them said out loud is like 'decayed', meaning rotten

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles that these are bad times, and one period sounds it.
explanation.walkthrough: The singular of the answer is pronounced much like 'decayed', a synonym for rotten.
explanation.definitionFit: Ten-year periods are spans of time, the times of the clue.

clue.text: Ran into Bismarck in a Gothic castle.

indicators.note: into says the first word goes inside the chancellor's first name

parts.note: Otto von Bismarck was the German chancellor

explanation.surface: A German chancellor bumps into someone in a spooky castle.
explanation.walkthrough: Horace Walpole's The Castle of Otranto (1764) is held to be the first Gothic novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Walpole's novel The Castle of Otranto founded Gothic fiction, so the place names that eerie fortress.

clue.text: Obsolete love vessel holds two

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

indicators.note: holds says the vessel contains the next word

parts.note: an urn is a vessel
taken as written

explanation.surface: An outdated romantic vessel containing a couple.
explanation.definitionFit: Something no longer in use is out of date, worn out past usefulness.

clue.text: A convenience to many a weaver ?

parts.note: a convenience is a public lavatory, a loo
M is a thousand in Roman numerals, hence many

explanation.surface: A public toilet that many weavers find handy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'convenience' means a toilet (British, as in 'public convenience'); M (1000) for 'many' is a crossword convention.
explanation.definitionFit: The machine that interlaces threads into cloth is the device doing the weaving, a mechanical weaver.

clue.text: Rate this land part of our kingdom

definitions.meaning: ... is an old word for a tax or levy, as in ...-free

definitions.text: this land part of our kingdom
definitions.meaning: add the word land to this one and you get a part of the United Kingdom

explanation.definitionFit: An old tax or levy survives in 'scot-free', and the same word followed by 'land' names a country in the UK.

clue.text: The front is false, appearIng shaky

definitions.meaning: weak or unreliable, as in a dodgy heart

explanation.definitionFit: A detachable false shirt-front has this name, and in British slang the word also means feeble or unsound.

clue.text: "Fain would I ——" wrote Sir Walter

parts.note: Sir Walter Raleigh scratched on a window 'Fain would I ___, yet fear I to fall'; the missing verb means to ascend

explanation.surface: A quotation from Sir Walter with its key word left blank.
explanation.walkthrough: Raleigh wrote the line on a window; Queen Elizabeth replied 'If thy heart fails thee, climb not at all'.
explanation.definitionFit: Raleigh's line is about ambition, wanting to rise at court, to go up.

clue.text: Home for the whipper of her numerous progeny

definitions.text: Home for the whipper of her numerous progeny

parts.words: Home for the whipper of her numerous progeny
parts.note: the nursery-rhyme old woman with so many children she didn't know what to do whipped them all soundly and put them to bed; she lived in a piece of footwear

explanation.surface: Where a harsh mother of a huge brood lives.
explanation.walkthrough: The rhyme: 'There was an old woman who lived in a ___, she had so many children she didn't know what to do'.
explanation.definitionFit: In the nursery rhyme the old woman with many children lived in an item of footwear.

clue.text: Score not followed by the church

indicators.note: followed by places the second piece straight after the first

parts.note: CH is the usual abbreviation for church

explanation.surface: A tally that is not followed by the church.
explanation.definitionFit: A score is a cut or nick, the same as a small V-shaped cut made for counting.

clue.text: Appropriate size for small book on grouse-shooting?

definitions.text: Appropriate size for small book on grouse-shooting?

parts.words: Appropriate size for small book on grouse-shooting?
parts.note: grouse-shooting opens on the Glorious Twelfth of August, so the fitting book format is the one named after twelve

explanation.surface: A publisher asks what format suits a little book about shooting grouse.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain grouse-shooting opens on 12 August, 'the Glorious Twelfth'; this book size has leaves folded into twelve.
explanation.definitionFit: A small book format with each sheet folded into twelve leaves takes its name from the Latin for twelve.

clue.text: Can be gentle as birds preening themselves at it?

definitions.text: Can be gentle as birds preening themselves at it?

parts.words: Can be gentle as birds preening themselves at it?
parts.note: the birds are women (British slang) getting ready, preening before a mirror at a piece of bedroom furniture

explanation.surface: Birds can be gentle as they groom their feathers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'birds' is British slang for young women; preening is making up and tidying the hair.
explanation.definitionFit: A bedroom table with a mirror is where people sit to make themselves up and do their hair.
